title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Afghanistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Afghanistan: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Afghanistan: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: Preparing healthcare, legal representation, and family financial records in advance for someone living with serious or terminal illness in Afghanistan requires practical local planning because, following institutional disruption and the absence of accessible functioning state web portals under de facto administration, domestic civil-registry and court websites (including the National Statistics and Information Authority portal) are offline or unreachable from abroad [1][5][8]. To provide verifiable guidance where domestic digital services are down, statutory background on the 1977 Civil Code, population registration, labour law, and disability legislation is anchored here in verified international archives (FAOLEX, WIPO Lex, UNHCR Refworld, and ILO NATLEX) alongside foreign civil-document reciprocity and diplomatic mission pages (travel.state.gov, GOV.UK, UNHCR, and accredited Afghan missions), advising in-person verification at local municipal or district offices or accredited diplomatic missions [1][2][3][4][6].

steps.title: Healthcare documentation, consent, and identity preparedness
steps.html:
• Medical records and hospital consent practice: Hospitals under the Ministry of Public Health and Disability Care Authorities in Afghanistan do not maintain a nationwide digital advance-directive registry; recording treatment wishes in writing with the attending physician and naming one primary family representative reduces confusion during acute care [2][5].
  • Securing a Tazkira or e-Tazkira early: Under the Law on Registration of Population Records (2014), the Tazkira (paper ID or biometric e-Tazkira) is essential to verify identity, bank access, and property ownership; UNHCR and UK Home Office reporting notes major gender gaps in Tazkira possession and male-chaperone (mahram) accompaniment rules when women apply in person [4][5][8].
  • Documenting witness and community ties: Because domestic records frequently depend on attestation by community leaders (Maliks or Wakil-e Guzars) and two adult witnesses, keeping certified copies of family Tazkiras and hospital files together streamlines future administrative steps [1][5].

steps.title: Powers of attorney (Wakalat) and mission accessibility limits
steps.html:
• Domestic court execution: Inside Afghanistan, granting a representative authority to manage bank accounts, pension matters, or property requires executing a formal Power of Attorney before Local Courts (Mahkama) and Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department in Kabul while the principal has full mental capacity [2][3][6].
  • Consular execution for diaspora families: Principals abroad who need an agent in Afghanistan must check which missions currently issue valid documents; functioning Accredited Afghan Diplomatic Missions Abroad (Consular Power of Attorney Services) such as the Embassy in Vienna require an in-person appointment, two Afghan or Muslim adult male witnesses with IDs, and subsequent in-country certification by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department in Kabul [6][8].
  • Capacity boundaries: Under Afghan Civil Code agency principles, an ordinary Power of Attorney ceases upon loss of capacity or interdiction, making early notarization vital before cognitive deterioration [2][3].

steps.title: Wills, 1977 Civil Code succession rules, and deed readiness
steps.html:
• Civil Code Articles 1993 to 2197: Estate transmission is governed by the Civil Code of the Republic of Afghanistan (1977) (Articles 1993 to 2197), establishing mandatory Sharia-aligned shares for spouses, children, parents, and close relatives (with sons generally inheriting double the share of daughters) [2][3].
  • One-third testamentary rule: Under Afghan civil and Islamic law principles, a written will (Wasiyat) can allocate up to one-third of the net estate to non-heirs or charitable causes; larger dispositions or alterations to statutory shares require unanimous consent from adult heirs [2][3].
  • Organizing property deeds (Qabala) and bank accounts: Gathering original court-registered land deeds (Qabala), witness-signed property papers, and bank records ahead of time protects household tenure and speeds up eventual Hasr-e Werathat proceedings [1][3][5].

steps.title: Disability benefits, employment leave, and welfare disruption
steps.html:
• Labour Law protections: Insured formal employees undergoing extended medical treatment are covered by sick-leave and medical-certificate rules under Afghanistan's Labour Law (No. 35 of 2007), though formal private-sector enforcement remains narrow [7].
  • Disability rights framework and fiscal limits: Statutory entitlements for medical rehabilitation and allowances exist on paper under the Law on Rights and Benefits of Disabled Persons overseen by the Ministry of Public Health and Disability Care Authorities in Afghanistan, but humanitarian reporting highlights severe post-2021 budget and administrative interruptions [8][9].
  • Supplementing with community and NGO health support: Because state welfare disbursements are unreliable, families frequently supplement medical documentation with provincial hospital social-work referrals and international humanitarian assistance programs [5][8].

steps.title: Civil-registry alignment and consular legalization (non-Apostille)
steps.html:
• Synchronizing Tazkira, passport, and deed names: Confirming identical transliteration and parent lineage details across passports, paper Tazkiras, and e-Tazkiras held at Municipal, District, and Provincial Civil Registration Offices (Tazkira / NSIA) avoids later document rejections [1][4][5].
  • Non-Apostille treaty status: According to the Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH) status table, Afghanistan is not a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention; Apostille certificates have no legal effect for Afghanistan [10].
  • Consular legalization requirements: Medical reports, notarized Powers of Attorney, and civil records moving internationally require sequential consular legalization through Local Courts (Mahkama) and Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department in Kabul and Accredited Afghan Diplomatic Missions Abroad (Consular Power of Attorney Services) plus receiving-country embassies where available [1][6][10].

closingQuestion: Are you preparing local medical and court documents inside Afghanistan, or arranging a witnessed Power of Attorney at an Afghan diplomatic mission abroad?

prefillQuestion: A family member is facing a serious or terminal illness in Afghanistan. We need an overview of the main official steps and contacts in Afghanistan for palliative care, powers of attorney, advance directives, and caregiver support.

contacts.name: Accredited Afghan Diplomatic Missions Abroad (Consular Power of Attorney Services)
contacts.note: Operational Afghan embassies issuing Powers of Attorney in person with two Afghan or Muslim adult male witnesses for certification in Kabul.

contacts.name: Local Courts (Mahkama) and Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department in Kabul
contacts.note: Domestic primary courts handling wills, deeds, and Powers of Attorney, and Kabul MFA department certifying overseas consular POAs.

contacts.name: Municipal, District, and Provincial Civil Registration Offices (Tazkira / NSIA)
contacts.note: District and municipal authorities processing Tazkira, e-Tazkira, and vital population records under the 2014 Population Registration Law.

contacts.name: Ministry of Public Health and Disability Care Authorities in Afghanistan
contacts.note: Hospitals and disability assessment authorities managing medical documentation and statutory disability entitlements.
